author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution first builds a **prefix-sum array** `dp` where `dp[i]` holds the running total of all digits in `s` up to index `i-1`, so the sum of digits in any range `[l, r]` can be computed instantly as `dp[r+1] - dp[l]`. For each query, it takes the substring `s[l..r]`, **strips out zeros** with `replace(/0/g, '')`, converts what's left to a `Number`, and multiplies that by the digit-sum of the range, taking the result `mod 1e9+7`. It fails because converting a long digit string directly to a plain JavaScript `Number` loses precision once the value exceeds `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so large substrings produce an incorrect concatenated value before the multiplication even happens.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is nearly identical to the first attempt: it uses a **prefix-sum array** `dp` to get the digit-sum of any range in O(1), then for each query strips zeros from the substring, converts it to a `Number`, and now takes `x % MOD` *before* multiplying by `sum`. This still fails because the bug isn't in the modulo step — it's that `Number(s.slice(l, r + 1).replace(/0/g, ''))` already loses precision for long digit strings before `% MOD` is ever applied, so `x` itself is wrong for large inputs.

aiExplanation: This version fixes the precision bug by switching to **`BigInt`**: it still uses a `dp` prefix-sum array for digit sums, but now converts the zero-stripped substring with `BigInt(...)` and does the multiplication and modulo (`MOD = 10n ** 9n + 7n`) using big-integer arithmetic so large numbers stay exact. It gets the right answer but times out because, for every query, it re-slices and re-parses a potentially very long substring of `s` and strips its zeros from scratch — with many queries on a long string, this repeated `O(n)` work per query becomes too slow overall.

notes: I didn't fully understand the math that went into this solution, nor did I have the time to really look at it.
aiExplanation: This accepted solution avoids re-scanning substrings entirely by precomputing three **prefix arrays** in one pass over `s`: `dpSum` (running digit sum), `dpLen` (running count of *non-zero* digits), and `dpX` (the value you'd get by concatenating all non-zero digits so far, kept modulo `1e9+7` using `BigInt`). It also precomputes `pow10`, powers of 10 mod `MOD`, up front. For each query `[l, r]`, it finds how many non-zero digits lie before `l` (`dpLen[l]`) to know how far to "shift" `dpX[l]` with `pow10[len]`, then subtracts that shifted prefix from `dpX[r+1]` to isolate the concatenated value for just the `[l, r]` range — turning what used to be `O(n)` per query into **`O(1)`**, which is why it now runs fast enough to pass.
